🐛 Bug
torch.jit.isinstance will falsely return True in eager when comparing any two container types that are the same, even if those types don't have the same subscript. My guess is that we silently transform List[T] into list for the eager mode check, which is not correct. The example below demonstrates that torch.jit.isinstance recognizes List[T1] as an instance of List[T2] since both types are Lists, even if T1 and T2 are invariant.
This is not a problem in script mode.
Example
import torch
from typing import List

def fn():
    x: List[torch.Tensor] = []
    if torch.jit.isinstance(x, List[int]):
        print("Wrong!")
    else:
        print("Right")
    return x

scripted = torch.jit.script(fn)
scripted()                 # prints "Right"
fn()                       # prints "Wrong!"
cc @gmagogsfm
nodes.title: `torch.jit.isinstance` is overly admissive when comparing container types in eager mode

🚀 Feature
I would love to see a pytorch implementation of LDL (Bunch-Kaufman) decomposition.
Motivation
LDL is a great alternative to Cholesky for symmetric/hermitian matrices that are not positive definite. At the moment, pytorch's only alternative factorization for hermitian matrices is eigendecomposition (e.g. torch.symeig and torch.linalg.eigh). In my experience, eigh is much slower and does not scale to batch as Cholesky does (and as LDL in theory should).
Pitch
LDL can be implemented using LAPACK's sytrf and hetrf routines (a la scipy.linalg). For CUDA, there is a working implementation in the cuSolver library.

🐛 Bug
The first call to caffe2::CUDAContext::SwitchToDevice(0) will ignore the default CUDA Stream and acquire a new low priority CUDA Stream and set this stream as the new current stream for the given device.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Run trace that allocates memory using the default stream and subsequently calls into caffe2::CUDAContext::SwitchToDevice()
Run the trace again any amount of times
Observe that the subsequent runs of the trace allocate memory from a stream that is not the default stream. CUDACachingAllocator is not able to re-use the memory allocated from the first execution because it was allocated from a separate stream.

Additional context
The constructor of caffe2::ThreadLocalCUDAObjects initializes a vector of CUDA stream for each GPU in the cuda_streams_ member variable. These vectors are all initialized to empty and populated on subsequent calls to caffe2::ThreadLocalCUDAObjects::GetCUDAStream. One such code path is from the call stack shown above. Specifically, caffe2::CUDAContext::SwitchToDevice(0) is called from context_base.h#L48 (via context_gpu.h#L180) with the apparent intention to use the default stream (based on notes in PR #15126). However, this code path triggers a call to c10::cuda::getStreamFromPool from within caffe2::ThreadLocalCUDAObjects::GetCUDAStream due to the fact that the caffe2::ThreadLocalCUDAObjects::cuda_streams_ member has no reference to the default stream. This causes a new stream to be acquired (as per tensor_cuda_stream documentation).
It seems that either the cuda_streams_ member variable should be initialized to include the default stream, or GetCUDAStream should check for logical stream id 0 and call getDefaultCUDAStream instead of getStreamFromPool.

🚀 Feature
Add support for users to attach parameter names to the tensor and thus make the names available to the C++ back-propagation code. Modify selected DDP C++ RuntimeError messages to include the parameter name of the tensor that triggered the error.
Motivation
The error messages from the C++ layer of PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) are less helpful than they could be, as they are unable to name the specific parameter which triggered the error. For example:
RuntimeError: Expected to mark a variable ready only once.
rather than something like:
RuntimeError: Variable decoders.2.1.response_decoder.layer_0.ff.weight: Expected to mark a variable ready only once.
Another similar error message is:
RuntimeError: Expected to have finished reduction in the prior iteration before starting a new one. This error indicates that your module has parameters that were not used in producing loss.
It would be really helpful to report the names of the parameters that were not used in producing loss.
Pitch
I've modified PyTorch to enable the user to attach the model parameter names to the Variable portion of the tensors (the AutogradMeta struct) so that the C++ code can access the parameter name for use in error messages, and modified the first error message above to include the parameter name.
Alternatives
I'm open to suggestions. Trolling though the torchviz graphs really didn't give me enough insight to find my problem.
Additional context
In my implementation, I planned to add a new parameter_name member to struct AutogradMeta, but I ended up hacking it to re-use the existing name member. I gather this would probably break the JIT and Caffe2.
It would be preferable to not require the user to explicitly add the parameter names to the tensors, but the full parameter name isn't known until after the user has constructed the full model. Perhaps the first forward pass could add the annotations?

@pbelevich reported that when calling rref = rpc.remote("dst", model.forward) with CUDA RPC on an expensive model, the following rref.to_here() might not fetch the correct result. This is because  rpc.remote and rref.to_here are two separate request/response pairs and they don't share CUDA streams. So, with our current implementation, rref.to_here might read the result before it's ready.

I am thinking about passing a list of devices when invoking the RPC request callback. Then rpc.remote related processors can retrieve that list and record one CUDAEvent on each device and store those CUDAEvents on the RRef. Later, when rref.to_here() is executed on the callee, the RRef can use the recorded CUDAEvents to block current streams on those devices.

🚀 Feature
Currently there does not appear to be any way to @torch.jit.ignore an @property on a module that is not compatible with TorchScript. Sometimes a Module may expose some (derived object of) its initialization arguments as immutable @propertys, but those objects may be incompatible with TorchScript.
Motivation
In [1]: import torch

In [9]: class M(torch.nn.Module):
   ...:     @property
   ...:     def func(self):
   ...:         return lambda x: x * 2
   ...: 

In [10]: m = M()

In [11]: m.func(2)
Out[11]: 4

In [12]: ms = torch.jit.script(m)

UnsupportedNodeError: Lambda aren't supported:
  File "<ipython-input-9-4ec6558e83af>", line 4
    @property
    def func(self):
        return lambda x: x * 2
               ~ <--- HERE

In [13]: class M(torch.nn.Module):
    ...:     @torch.jit.ignore
    ...:     @property
    ...:     def func(self):
    ...:         return lambda x: x * 2
    ...: 

RuntimeError: Argument to @torch.jit.ignore must be a bool or a function but got <property object at 0x7f1393a5f130>

In [14]: class M(torch.nn.Module):
    ...:     @property
    ...:     @torch.jit.ignore
    ...:     def func(self):
    ...:         return lambda x: x * 2
    ...: 

In [15]: m = M()

In [16]: m.func(2)

  File "<ipython-input-14-e11b332e46b5>", line 5
    @torch.jit.ignore
    def func(self):
        return lambda x: x * 2
               ~ <--- HERE
Pitch
Add support for property objects to @torch.jit.ignore
OR
Just ignore all @propertys in TorchScript (possibly unless they are decorated with @torch.jit.export.)
Alternatives
One can remove @propertys from the module and use normal, mutable attributes instead. (Requires source changes.) This approach is still incompatible with type-annotated attributes, see #53753.

Today, when serializing TorchScript code we make no distinction between arguments that were explicitly specified by the user, and arguments that can from defaults. This leads us to "burn in" default arguments.
This behavior causes forward compatibility problems when a new argument with a default value is added to an operator. Consider:
# version 1
aten.foo(Tensor arg1)

becoming
# version 2
aten.foo(Tensor arg1, String new_arg="my_default_value")

The serialized code at version 2 looks like:
aten.foo(my_tensor_input, "my_default_value")

so when you try to run it in a binary at version 1, you get a "too many arguments for schema" error.
One option is to not serialize the default value, so then the serialized code at version 2 looks like:
aten.foo(my_tensor_input)  # the schema matcher will insert new_arg="my_default_value"

and thus we retain compatibility.
This is a practically important issue, currently adding a new default value to a custom op will break PyPER due to forward compat issues: https://fburl.com/3fr2kjvn
cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @bdhirsh @jbschlosser @anjali411 @gmagogsfm

Hi, we would like to discuss the PyTorch adoption of the recently proposed array-api: https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/.
We are aware of the proposal in #54138 to adopt __array_interface__ in the PyTorch tensor but its main purpose seems to be eliminating the current PyTorch and numpy dependency.
Motivation
The array API is similar to the __array_interface__ but extended beyond the realms of NumPy and providing support for accelerators. So it will ease the portability and reduce the burden of having to manage different interfaces such as DLPack or array interface depending on the device the array resides in.
We are wondering if support for this API would be welcomed in PyTorch and we would like to actively develop it since we are also planning to implement this in CuPy and both projects could benefit from this.
Discussion points
One of the most important points to discuss is how would be adding support for this. Adding a submodule to ensure compatibility? in the same way that tensorflow added numpy compatibility tensorflow.experimental.numpy.

🚀 Feature

ROCm support should be in what you get from pip install torch, or from another package listing torch as a requirement.
Motivation

If I'm writing (or running) downstream tools that use PyTorch, I don't care if it does its compute on an nVidia GPU via CUDA or on an AMD GPU via ROCm. I need just generic GPU-accelerated PyTorch as a dependency. Right now, with the ROCm version hosted separately, it seems impossible to have a setup.py that will depend on the version appropriate to the locally available hardware, plus I don't think anything in PyPI is allowed to depend on packages outside of PyPI and pull them in automatically.
Pitch

The PyPI torch module should support both ROCm and CUDA in the same wheel, and ideally magically select whichever is appropriate to use at runtime.
Alternatives

ROCm (and CUDA?) could be [extras], so you could pip install torch[rocm], pip install torch[cuda], or, assuming the combination is actually possible, pip install torch[rocm,cuda].
Additional context

I saw PyTorch 1.8 added ROCm support, according to Phoronix. I pip install torch'd and got 1.8. I did not get ROCm support and was upset and confused.
It's also confusing that pytorch.cuda is where the ROCm-backed API lives when you are running on ROCm. I suppose that's necessary to run existing workloads, but the docs should then make it clear that the cuda module doesn't necessarily have anything to do with CUDA itself, depending on installation configuration. In reality, "ROCm" appears once in the 1.8 docs, on the page about people in a heading.
